name: Yara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a 250-tonne excavator at the Whitestone lithium mine, digging ore and loading the trucks. I'm senior operator on my crew, so I do the dig plan with the geologist each morning and keep the grade right, which means not mixing waste rock into the ore. I love the precision of it, people think it's brute force, but a good operator can peel a two-metre layer off like a potato. What wears me out is four nights in a row, and the drive home along the long straight stretch where I always nearly fall asleep.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Lukas on his family's sheep farm outside Whitestone, in the old shearers' cottage. On my days off I run my own little earthmoving business with a used five-tonne mini-excavator I bought on finance last year, house pads, farm dams, trenches. Between the finance payments and Whitestone paying below the other lithium mines, I've got about two weeks of money in the account. I use AI every day for the business, quotes, invoices, even working out how much dirt is in a dam wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep doing what I'm doing, which is fine. The AI's already paying for itself in my little business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people should stop being scared of it. It does my quotes in five minutes instead of an hour on a Sunday night. I'd say that at church, actually, some of the farmers still do their books in pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's fine for me but a bit of a missed chance. I like new things, and I'd been half hoping for more. But slow and steady suits a girl with a finance bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the mine job for the steady money and grow the weekend business, maybe from three jobs a month to five. I'd pay the mini-ex off a year early if I could. And I'd keep using AI for all the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even. Nothing's being taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about one of those weekend jobs.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month Mrs Hollis wanted a dam cleaned out before summer. I got the AI to estimate the silt volume from my drone photos, quoted her 1,800 dollars, and did it in a day and a half. She paid in cash and gave me a lamb roast, which is the best kind of tip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the mine job at all, if the business is going well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the business is two weeks of savings and one broken track away from trouble. The mine pays the finance, the business pays for the future. I'm not silly enough to jump before I've got a cushion.

S0.say: It's a good tool and people should stop being scared of it; it does my quotes in five minutes instead of an hour. I'd say that at church to the farmers still doing books in pencil.
S0.think: It's fine for me but a bit of a missed chance, because I like new things. Still, slow and steady suits someone with a finance bill.
S0.do: Keeps the mine job for steady pay and grows her weekend earthmoving business from three to five jobs a month. Aims to pay off the mini-excavator a year early and keeps using AI for all paperwork.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, with nothing being taken away.
S0.quote: She paid in cash and gave me a lamb roast, which is the best kind of tip.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is both a senior mine operator and a small business owner, and AI is already part of her side business. She's careful not to leave the mine before she has a cushion. Her church and farming community shape how she talks about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's exciting, honestly. Whitestone's already talking about a semi-autonomous digger trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board early, because the people who learn the new gear first get the good jobs. I'd say don't wait for the government or the union to save you, nobody owes us a job. That might not make me popular at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's my chance. If Whitestone puts in remote diggers, I want to be the first operator they train. And I'd look at whether I can put a guidance kit on my own mini-ex, so I can do more jobs with less of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the mine manager and ask to be on the trial. I'd look at a GPS machine-guidance kit for the mini-ex, about 9,000 dollars, and work out if the extra jobs would pay it off in a year. If the numbers worked, I'd borrow for it, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit fired up. Like the first dig on a new bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Borrowing 9,000 more on two weeks of savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd only do it if I'd already booked enough jobs to cover it. I'd sit down with Lukas and the spreadsheet first. Risk isn't the problem, being stupid about risk is the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Tony on the other digger. He's 59 and he's wonderful, but he still calls the tablet 'that television'. I'd hope they let him run the old machine till he retires, out of respect.

S1.say: Get on board early, because those who learn the new gear first get the good jobs. Don't wait for government or the union, because nobody owes us a job.
S1.think: It's my chance to be the first operator trained on remote diggers. I'd also look at a guidance kit for my own mini-excavator so I can do more jobs with less of me.
S1.do: Asks the mine manager to join the autonomous digger trial right away. Considers borrowing about 9,000 dollars for a GPS guidance kit on her mini-excavator, only if booked jobs already cover it.
S1.feel: Calm and fired up, like the first dig on a new bench.
S1.quote: Risk isn't the problem, being stupid about risk is the problem.
S1.fieldNote: Yara wants to automate her own small business as well as be first in line at the mine. Her free-market view is blunt about nobody owing anyone a job, but she wants respect for older colleagues like Tony. She's careful about debt despite liking risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's the one where my little business gets hit too, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, and people need to lean on their families and churches, not wait for a handout. Farms will still need people who know the land for a while. I'd tell people not to sit and wait, to find the next thing early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried, more than I'd let on. If robots can dig a farm dam in 2028, my mini-ex is worth half of what I owe on it. Two weeks of savings and a finance bill is a bad place to be in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the mini-ex in the first few months, before every other operator tries to sell theirs and the price drops. I'd keep the mine job as long as it lasts and bank every cent. Lukas and I would move from the cottage into the main house with his parents to save, and I'd put my hands into the farm, which needs work anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I'm steering, but the road's gone slippery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I sell, I don't build. In a longer one I'd buy robots for my own business and ride it. Here, there's no time for the business to pay back anything, so the smart move is to get out of debt fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Lukas's parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His mum would be thrilled and I'd be climbing the walls by week three. But that's what families are for. My nan always said you don't count favours inside a family, you just do them.

S2.say: It'll be hard, and people need to lean on family and church rather than wait for a handout. Farms will still need people who know the land, so find the next thing early.
S2.think: I'd be more worried than I'd let on. If robots dig farm dams by 2028, my mini-excavator is worth half what I owe, with two weeks of savings.
S2.do: Sells the mini-excavator in the first few months before used prices fall, keeps the mine job as long as it lasts and banks everything. Moves with her partner into his parents' farmhouse to save rent and starts working on the farm.
S2.feel: Anxious but still steering, on a road gone slippery.
S2.quote: Two years means I sell, I don't build.
S2.fieldNote: Yara's adaptability shows as speed: she'd sell her machine early to avoid being caught with debt. Her traditional values point her to family and church for support. The farm offers a fallback that most of her colleagues don't have, which keeps her short of alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to make some money out of it before it lands, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's five years to get ahead, so get ahead. Learn the new gear, start something, buy the right machine early. I'd say waiting for someone else to sort it out is the worst plan there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the first three years could be the best years I've had. Everyone will want earthmoving done with the new guided machines and there won't be enough operators who know them. After 2031, I don't know, but I'd have made something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd fit the guidance kit to the mini-ex and push the weekend business to six or eight jobs a month. I'd get on the autonomous trial at Whitestone. By year two, I'd think about going full-time on my own, if I had three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and mostly excited, but there's a clock ticking in the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years, compared with two, change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They flip it. With two years I'm selling the machine. With five I'm buying the kit and making it pay. Same end point, completely different first move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After 2031, what would you want to have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No debt and a paid-off machine, at least. Maybe some land of our own next to Lukas's family. Land doesn't get automated, it just sits there being land.

S3.say: There are five years to get ahead, so get ahead: learn the new gear, start something, buy the right machine early. Waiting for someone else to sort it is the worst plan.
S3.think: The first three years could be my best ever, with demand for guided machines and few operators who know them. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd have built something.
S3.do: Fits a guidance kit to her mini-excavator in year one and grows weekend work to six or eight jobs a month while joining the mine's autonomous trial. Considers going full-time on her own by year two once she has three months saved.
S3.feel: Uneasy, busy and mostly excited, with a clock ticking in the background.
S3.quote: Land doesn't get automated, it just sits there being land.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years flip her first move from selling to investing. She sees a short window of high demand for operators of guided machines. Her long-term hope is land and no debt, a traditional kind of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole business, start to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the AGI pictures, and anyone who plans can come out fine. Start a business, learn the tools, look after your family. I'd say the government's job is mostly to stay out of the way and keep apprenticeships cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'd come out ahead in this one. Ten years is enough to build a small earthmoving company with two or three guided machines, then sell it before the full robots arrive. That's the plan forming in my head already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the mine job for two more years, save up three months, then go full-time on the business with the guided mini-ex. By year five I'd buy a second machine and hire a young operator, maybe one of Lukas's cousins. Lukas and I would get married at the church in town once I'm full-time, and think about kids after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. This is the version where being early pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the business before the full robots arrive. How would you know when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch the big contractors. When they start buying fully autonomous diggers in bulk, the small guys have maybe two years left. That's when I'd sell to one of them, while my customer list is still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier nobody owes us a job. Does that apply to your young operator too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. No, I'd owe him a proper apprenticeship and an honest heads-up when I'm selling. That's different from the government owing people, that's just being a decent boss.

S4.say: This is the best of the AGI pictures, and anyone who plans can come out fine. Government's job is mostly to stay out of the way and keep apprenticeships cheap.
S4.think: I'd come out ahead: ten years is enough to build a small earthmoving company with guided machines and sell it before full robots arrive.
S4.do: Keeps the mine job for two more years to save three months, then goes full-time with her guided mini-excavator. Buys a second machine and hires a young operator by year five, and plans a church wedding once she's full-time.
S4.feel: Calm and excited; being early pays off in this one.
S4.quote: When they start buying fully autonomous diggers in bulk, the small guys have maybe two years left.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Yara has a complete business plan including when to sell. When challenged on her own line that nobody owes anyone a job, she accepts that a boss owes an apprentice training and honesty. Marriage and children come after the business is established.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it catches me with debt on a machine nobody will want. What would help is a way to sell or hand back equipment without losing everything, maybe the finance companies giving people a fair way out. And cheap short courses for whatever comes next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot on my own machine, and the answer is yes, if I own it. A robot that works for me is a business. A robot that works instead of me is a problem.

headlineQuote: A robot that works for me is a business. A robot that works instead of me is a problem.
portrait: Yara Bauer is a 27-year-old senior excavator operator at a lithium mine who also runs a weekend earthmoving business with a mini-excavator bought on finance, living with her partner Lukas on his family's sheep farm on two weeks of savings. She uses AI every day for quotes and invoices and sees technology as opportunity. She's calm through the plateau and steady pictures, eager to join the autonomous trial and automate her own machine. Two-year AGI makes her anxious and pushes her to sell the machine early and lean on Lukas's family, while five and ten years let her build, and plan to sell, a small business. Her traditional, free-market views shape her focus on family, church and owning the robots rather than being replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would catch her owing money on a machine nobody would want.
whatWouldHelp: A fair way to sell or hand back financed equipment without losing everything, and cheap short courses for whatever comes next.
